executive_summary: Assessment asm-001 examined ForgeFlow, a GitHub-integrated service in which webhook events drive queued analysis jobs, an analysis worker sends requests to an external AI provider, and results are stored and published as pull-request comments. Eight documents were supplied — ai-analysis.md, architecture-overview.md, github-integration.md, operations-guide.md, product-overview.md, sample-repository-notes.md, security-overview.md and structured-system-input.yaml — and every one of them was reviewed and ingested, so their evidence was available to each stage of the analysis. The assessment produced four approved findings: two that the reviewer assigned high severity, fnd-001 (forged or replayed webhook deliveries creating analysis jobs for installations the sender does not control) and fnd-002 (instruction-bearing repository content driving customer source content into an externally visible pull-request comment); and two that the reviewer assigned medium severity, fnd-004 (restricted source content and prompts reaching shared logging and diagnostic artifacts) and fnd-005 (one tenant's event volume or retry behaviour exhausting shared analysis capacity). Five controls were confirmed as supported by evidence: the access restriction on the managed Redis queue, the managed secrets service holding integration credentials, delegated customer authentication to GitHub with ForgeFlow-held membership and roles, platform-provided encryption of stored artifacts together with TLS for customer traffic, and independent horizontal scaling of receivers and workers with Redis buffering and degraded-mode result access. No documentation gaps were approved. A substantial amount remains undetermined nonetheless: twenty-six open questions are recorded, twelve of them high severity, covering among other things how inbound webhook requests are validated and how replayed deliveries are handled, what enforces authorization on the managed object storage bucket and how time-limited links are scoped, what implements the documented repository-content instruction boundary, whether publication of AI-derived comments involves any human review step, whether API authorization is deny-by-default for customer resources, whether ForgeFlow operations personnel can read customer source artifacts and prompts, and which of two conflicting statements is authoritative for artifact retention and for the requirements identified as req-AI-002 and req-DATA-002. Each of the four findings records its requirement as partially satisfied for the threat it addresses, and each recommendation asks that whether the requirement is met be established and that the control meeting it be recorded. Four approved findings and five confirmed controls are not a statement that ForgeFlow is secure; they are the conclusions the supplied evidence supported, bounded by the open questions above and by the limitations recorded at the end of this report.
system_overview: ForgeFlow, as described by the approved system context, is a multi-tenant service that receives GitHub events, performs AI-assisted analysis of repository content, and returns results both to a web interface and to customer pull requests. Customer browsers reach the system through a managed CDN and web application firewall, which serves a React web application; that application calls the ForgeFlow API, and customer users authenticate through a GitHub OAuth exchange. Event-driven work enters through a separate webhook receiver, which accepts GitHub webhook events and enqueues analysis jobs onto a managed Redis queue. An analysis worker polls and retrieves queued jobs, retrieves repository content from GitHub, sends analysis requests to an external AI provider, writes job metadata and structured results to managed PostgreSQL, stores artifacts in managed object storage, and triggers publication of a pull-request comment; a GitHub comment service publishes the summary comment back to GitHub. The API reads and writes customer records, retrieves artifacts and issues time-limited links to them, initiates selected GitHub API operations, and sends notifications through an email provider. An administrative interface, whose operators authenticate through a corporate identity provider, invokes ForgeFlow API operations. The API, the webhook receiver, the worker and the comment service all retrieve secrets from a managed secrets service, and each of those services, along with the administrative interface, forwards events or actions to a central logging platform. GitHub, the external AI provider, the email provider and the corporate identity provider are the external systems in scope. The actors recognised are customer developers and engineering users, customer or repository administrators, ForgeFlow administrators and operations personnel, the GitHub platform and the external AI provider as service identities, and the author of repository or pull-request content. The assets the context identifies are customer source code and repository content; structured analysis results; pull-request, repository and installation metadata; user identity, organization membership and role information; the GitHub App private key; short-lived GitHub installation tokens; AI-provider, OAuth, email and database credentials; the customer browser session; analysis artifacts in object storage; audit events and operational logs; and analysis processing availability itself. Eight trust boundaries were approved: the public internet boundary, the customer authentication boundary, the organization or tenant boundary, the GitHub boundary, the AI-provider boundary, the administrative privilege boundary, the secret-access boundary, and a repository-content instruction boundary separating ForgeFlow's own analysis instructions from untrusted repository and pull-request content. Documented controls sit across several of these: customer authentication is delegated to GitHub while ForgeFlow holds the organization membership and role information used for access decisions and maintains no local password database; integration credentials including the GitHub App private key are held in a managed secrets service and retrieved through workload identity where supported; the Redis queue is documented as reachable only from approved application workloads and not publicly accessible; stored customer data is encrypted by managed cloud storage services, with TLS documented for customer traffic and no application-implemented cryptography; and receiver and worker replicas scale independently with Redis buffering temporary spikes, with previously completed results remaining viewable during an AI-provider outage.
risk_summary: The four approved findings share a shape: in each case the requirement mapped to the threat is recorded as partially satisfied, and in each case the recommendation is to establish whether the requirement is met and to record the control that meets it. None of the four asserts that a control has been confirmed absent, and none is a documentation gap — no documentation gaps were approved — but together they concentrate on two themes. The first theme is the event-driven ingress path, where the two high-severity findings sit. fnd-001 concerns forged or replayed webhook deliveries creating analysis jobs for installations the sender does not control, with impact on analysis processing availability for other tenants, on written pull-request, repository and installation metadata for events that did not occur, and on unsolicited or duplicated comments appearing on customer pull requests under the ForgeFlow app identity. fnd-002 concerns instruction-bearing repository content driving customer source code and prompt or model artifacts into a pull-request comment and into the stored structured result; the reviewer recorded that the credential variant attempted by the injected text is weakened by the documented statement that credentials are not transmitted to the provider, so exposure is bounded by what is in the request. The second theme is restricted content and shared capacity crossing the tenant boundary in the processing path. fnd-004, at medium severity, concerns customer source content and prompt or model artifacts reaching audit and operational log stores whose access model is not the organization boundary. fnd-005, also medium, concerns one tenant's event volume or retry behaviour exhausting shared analysis capacity, degrading availability of new analysis for unrelated organizations while previously completed results remain viewable, which is the documented degraded-mode expectation. That last finding stands in direct relation to a confirmed control: the independent horizontal scaling of receivers and workers with Redis buffering is confirmed as a capacity measure that absorbs bursts, and the same evidence records that external AI-provider capacity may limit total throughput, so it does not bound consumption or protect one organization's throughput from another's load. Three of the four findings therefore describe restricted customer content or shared processing capacity crossing a boundary the documentation does not show being enforced, and the two high-severity findings both begin at content or events that arrive from outside ForgeFlow's control. The reviewer also recorded limitations against individual findings that qualify parts of them and should be read with them: crq-005 notes that the preconditions behind fnd-001 cover the forged branch of the attack path but not how a party comes to hold a previously delivered payload; crq-006 notes that the credited portion of the partially satisfied mapping for fnd-001 rests on the authenticated customer-request path and is attached to no named control, since the mapping's control list is empty; crq-013 notes that the assertion that pull requests may be visible to a wider audience than the ForgeFlow organization is not carried by the passages cited for it, and that the impact statement for fnd-002 leans on that widening; crq-043 notes that the exposure of short-lived installation tokens asserted in the impact of fnd-004 is not carried by the attack path as written; and crq-044 notes that the half of a precondition concerning error records derived from provider requests and responses is unsupported and cites an identifier that could not be resolved in that group's evidence. Beyond the findings, the open questions leave the surrounding posture undetermined rather than adverse. It could not be determined how inbound webhook requests are validated or whether replayed and duplicated deliveries are detected, what enforces authorization on the managed object storage bucket or how time-limited links are scoped and expired, what implements the documented repository-content instruction boundary or what handling is applied to AI output reflecting injected instructions, whether a human review step precedes comment publication, whether API organization scoping is enforced centrally and deny-by-default, or whether ForgeFlow operations personnel can read customer source artifacts and constructed prompts. Questions also ask which of two statements is authoritative for artifact retention and for the requirements identified as req-AI-002 and req-DATA-002, and further questions leave internal transport encryption, administrative multi-factor enforcement, session issuance and revocation, AI-provider retention and processing regions, retry and dead-letter behaviour, output encoding, object-storage network reachability, deployment pipeline authentication and dependency provenance, deletion scope across stores, and duplicate-job idempotency unresolved. These are open questions, not findings: they mark places where the answer would change the assessment and where the supplied documents did not settle it.

limitations.text: Finding fnd-001 rests on a stated assumption rather than on settled documentation, and the finding must be read with it. As recorded by the assessment: the receiver is documented as 'identifying the related installation and repository' (evd-028); whether that identification is a lookup against ForgeFlow-held installation records or acceptance of the payload identifiers is not stated, and the conclusion here rests on that being unstated rather than on it being wrong. If a reviewer can establish which of those two mechanisms the receiver actually performs, the basis of the finding changes accordingly.

Finding fnd-005 likewise rests on a stated assumption rather than on settled documentation. As recorded by the assessment: assumed that 'selected rate-limiting state' held in Redis (evd-029) relates to some enforced limit somewhere in the pipeline; the passage names the state but not the limit, its scope, or its enforcement point, so the nature of that limit is treated as unestablished. Any conclusion about whether shared analysis capacity is bounded per tenant therefore depends on information the supplied documents did not provide.
